questions.q: Why does Theo brief the sale's overall results and the incident together, rather than treating the incident as a footnote?
options: Because leadership requires a separate meeting for every incident, no matter how small
Because the honest version of how the sale went is incomplete without the 85 minutes of degraded checkout and why it happened — it's one story, not two
Because Dana Whitfield specifically forbids summarizing good news on its own
Because the incident report legally must be read aloud in full
questions.explain: Theo treats the sale's results and the incident as one honest account, since separating them would understate what actually happened during the sale.

questions.q: How does the leadership briefing's structure differ from the Lesson 15 incident report's structure?
options: It's identical, timeline-first in both cases
The briefing leads with business impact before technical mechanism, while the incident report is timeline-first — because leadership's first real question is about business effect
The briefing omits the root cause entirely
The briefing is written entirely in Kubernetes YAML
questions.explain: Theo reorders the same underlying facts: business impact first, then the real mechanism in plain language, because that matches what Dana and Casey actually need to hear first.

questions.q: What specific claim does Theo avoid overstating in the briefing?
options: That the sale happened at all
That fixing and validating checkout-api means no other service in the cluster has the same missing-constraint gap
That the FinOps dashboard exists
That Casey Lindqvist was involved in the incident
questions.explain: checkout-api is fixed and validated; that is a different claim from "every other service is also free of this gap," and the broader review is still an open follow-up action.

questions.q: What is the hardest question Theo anticipates, and how does he handle it?
options: "Should we cancel future sales?" — he says yes
"Why didn't the FinOps dashboard built to watch this catch it sooner?" — he names the dashboard's specific capacity-vs-reliability gap himself, before being asked
"Who should be blamed for this?" — he names a specific engineer
"How much did this cost in cloud spend?" — he refuses to answer
questions.explain: Theo proactively explains that the FinOps dashboard was built to answer a capacity/cost question, not a per-zone reliability one, and that Lesson 16's new panel and alert close exactly that gap.

questions.q: Why does proactively naming the FinOps dashboard's blind spot strengthen the briefing?
options: It doesn't — it would be better left unmentioned
Because naming the hard question himself, before it's raised as a challenge, keeps the conversation a briefing instead of a defense
Because it shifts blame onto the dashboard instead of the process
Because leadership will not notice the gap otherwise
questions.explain: Raising the hardest likely question directly, with the real answer already in hand, demonstrates the gap was understood and addressed rather than something leadership has to extract.
